Distributed Locks

1. What is a Distributed Lock?
  • A distributed lock provides mutual exclusion across all nodes in the cluster — only one thread on one node can hold the lock at a time;
  • It is the cluster-wide equivalent of Java's ReentrantLock;
  • Ignite implements it via IgniteLock (obtained from ignite.reentrantLock());
  • The lock state is stored inside a distributed cache, so it survives individual node failures (as long as backups are configured);
2. When to Use Distributed Locks
  • Leader election — ensure only one node performs a specific operation (e.g., scheduling, cleanup);
  • Protecting external resources — coordinate access to a shared file system, external API, or database that doesn't support concurrent writes;
  • One-time initialization — ensure a migration script or cache preload runs exactly once across the cluster;
  • Preventing duplicate processing — ensure only one node processes a specific event or message;
3. Creating and Using a Lock
  • // Parameters: name, failoverSafe, fair, create
IgniteLock lock = ignite.reentrantLock(
    "myDistributedLock",  // lock name (cluster-wide unique)
    true,                  // failoverSafe — auto-release if owner node fails
    true,                  // fair — FIFO ordering for waiting threads
    true                   // create — create if doesn't exist
);

lock.lock();
try {
    // Critical section — only one thread across the entire cluster runs this
    performExclusiveOperation();
} finally {
    lock.unlock();
}
4. Lock Parameters Explained
ParameterDescription
name Unique identifier for the lock across the cluster; all nodes requesting the same name compete for the same lock;
failoverSafe If true, the lock is automatically released when the node that holds it fails; prevents deadlocks on node crashes; if false, the lock becomes a broken barrier on node failure;
fair If true, threads acquire the lock in the order they requested it (FIFO); if false, no ordering guarantee (better throughput);
create If true, creates the lock if it doesn't already exist; if false, returns null when the lock doesn't exist;
5. Try-Lock with Timeout
  • Avoid blocking forever by using tryLock() with a timeout: 
    IgniteLock lock = ignite.reentrantLock("myLock", true, true, true);

if (lock.tryLock(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    try {
        // Acquired within 5 seconds
        performExclusiveOperation();
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
} else {
    // Could not acquire lock within 5 seconds
    System.out.println("Lock is busy — skipping or retrying");
}
6. Reentrant Behavior
  • Like Java's ReentrantLock, IgniteLock can be acquired multiple times by the same thread: 
    lock.lock();   // hold count = 1
lock.lock();   // hold count = 2 (same thread, reentrant)

lock.unlock(); // hold count = 1
lock.unlock(); // hold count = 0 (lock released)
  • Each lock() must be matched with an unlock();
7. Failover Behavior
  • With failoverSafe=true:
    • If the node holding the lock crashes, the lock is automatically released;
    • The next waiting thread (on another node) acquires the lock;
    • This prevents the entire cluster from deadlocking on a single node failure;
  • With failoverSafe=false:
    • If the owner node fails, all threads waiting on the lock receive a IgniteInterruptedException;
    • The lock becomes unusable until it is explicitly removed and recreated;
8. Removing a Lock
  • When a lock is no longer needed, close it to free cluster resources: 
    lock.close();  // removes the lock from the cluster
  • A closed lock cannot be used again — calling lock() will throw an exception;
9. Distributed Lock vs. Transactions vs. Entry Processors
MechanismUse WhenScope
IgniteLock Coordinating access to external resources or non-cache operations Cluster-wide, arbitrary code
Transactions Multi-key read-modify-write on cache data with ACID guarantees Cache entries only
Entry Processors Atomic read-modify-write on a single cache entry Single entry, runs on owning node
10. Best Practices
  • Always use failoverSafe=true in production to avoid cluster-wide deadlocks on node failure;
  • Always unlock in a finally block to prevent accidental lock leaks;
  • Prefer tryLock() with a timeout over lock() to avoid indefinite blocking;
  • Keep the critical section as short as possible — long-held locks reduce cluster throughput;
  • For cache-only operations, prefer transactions or entry processors over distributed locks — they are more efficient;
  • Use descriptive lock names to make debugging easier (e.g., "migration-lock", "report-generation-lock");
